title: Structs
summary: A **struct** is a typed collection of named fields grouped into one value — Go's way of modeling 'a thing with properties.' Structs are value types: assigning or passing one copies all its fields, which is central to how Go handles data without classes or inheritance.

subtopics.title: Declaring a struct type
subtopics.explanation: A struct type lists named fields with their types. The type name is usually capitalized when it should be exported. Each field has its own type and can be any type, including another struct.

subtopics.title: Struct literals & the zero value
subtopics.explanation: Create a struct with a literal: positional (User{1, "Ann"}) or — preferred — keyed (User{ID: 1, Name: "Ann"}). Keyed literals are robust to field reordering. A struct's zero value has every field set to its own zero value, so it is usable without initialization.
subtopics.example:
u := User{ID: 1, Name: "Ann"}
var empty User // {0 ""}

subtopics.title: Value semantics
subtopics.explanation: Structs are values. Assigning a struct, passing it to a function, or returning it copies every field. To let a function modify the original, pass a pointer (*User). This is why mutating methods take pointer receivers.
subtopics.example:
func rename(u User) { u.Name = "x" } // caller unaffected
func renamePtr(u *User) { u.Name = "x" } // modifies caller

subtopics.title: Embedding (composition)
subtopics.explanation: Go has no inheritance; instead you embed one struct in another to reuse fields and methods. The embedded type's fields and methods are promoted, so you can access them directly. This favors composition over inheritance.

subtopics.title: Comparability and tags
subtopics.explanation: Structs are comparable with == if all their fields are comparable; they can then be map keys. Field tags (backtick strings) attach metadata read by reflection, most commonly for JSON encoding.
subtopics.example:
type Point struct{ X, Y int }
Name string `json:"name"`

foundations.overview: A struct lets you bundle related data under one type — a User with an ID and a Name, a Point with X and Y. Go has no classes; structs plus methods plus interfaces are how you model the world. The single most important fact about structs is that they are value types: copying a struct copies all of its fields, which shapes how you pass data, write methods, and avoid surprising bugs.
foundations.formalDefinition: A struct is a composite type that aggregates zero or more named fields, each with its own type, into a single value with value (copy) semantics.
foundations.whyItMatters: Structs are the primary way to model domain data in Go. Understanding value semantics, the zero value, and embedding is essential for writing correct, idiomatic types and methods.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a labeled form with named blanks: each field is a blank with a fixed kind of answer. Making a copy of the form duplicates every filled-in blank; handing someone the original form (a pointer) lets them edit your copy.
foundations.runtimePerspective: A struct is laid out contiguously in memory, fields in declaration order, with padding inserted for alignment. There is no per-object header or vtable — a struct is just its fields packed together, which makes them cache-friendly and cheap to copy when small.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Modeling API request/response bodies, database rows, configuration, domain entities (User, Order, Account) — essentially every typed data record in a Go program.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear struct types make domain models self-documenting, reducing onboarding time and miscommunication between teams building against the same data shapes.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Value semantics prevent accidental shared-state bugs, but copying large structs in hot paths wastes CPU; choosing value vs pointer receivers correctly is a recurring design decision.
foundations.performanceImpact: Small structs are cheap to copy and stay on the stack; large structs copied frequently add CPU and memory-bandwidth cost, so they are often passed by pointer. Field ordering affects struct size via alignment padding.
commonUseCases: Composition via embedding instead of inheritance
Returning multiple related values as one typed result

commonMisconceptions.myth: Passing a struct to a function lets the function modify the original.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It receives a copy; only passing a pointer (*T) lets it modify the caller's value.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must initialize every field before using a struct.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The zero value sets each field to its own zero (0, "", nil), and that value is often immediately usable.
It is composition with field/method promotion; there is no subtype polymorphism — the outer type is not a subtype of the embedded one.

visualExplorer.caption: Why modifying a struct inside a by-value function leaves the caller's struct unchanged.

config.intro: Tracing a struct passed by value vs by pointer:

steps.name: Caller holds the struct
steps.detail: main has u := User{Name: "Ann"} — a value living in main's frame.

steps.name: Call by value copies fields
steps.detail: rename(u) copies every field into a new local u inside rename.

steps.name: The function mutates its copy
steps.detail: u.Name = "x" changes only the function's local copy, not main's.

steps.name: Caller is unchanged
steps.detail: Back in main, u.Name is still "Ann" — the mutation was lost.

steps.name: Pointer changes the rule
steps.detail: renamePtr(&u) passes the address; *u.Name = "x" reaches back and edits main's struct.

interactiveExamples.title: Declare, initialize, and read a struct
interactiveExamples.explanation: Keyed literals are the idiomatic way to build a struct. The zero value of a struct sets each field to its own zero, so var empty User prints {0 }.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the rename actually stick
interactiveExamples.explanation: The function receives a copy, so the caller's struct never changes. Edit the function and call site to use a pointer so the rename is visible in main.

checkpoints.explanation: Structs are values, so b := a copies all fields. Changing b.X does not affect a, which still has X = 1; b.X is 99.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the zero value of `var u struct{ ID int; Name string }`?
checkpoints.explanation: A struct's zero value sets each field to its own zero value: int to 0 and string to "". The result prints as {0 } and is safe to use immediately.

checkpoints.prompt: This positional literal compiles today but is fragile. Why?
options: If fields are reordered or added, the values silently map to the wrong fields
bool cannot be in a struct literal
checkpoints.explanation: Positional literals depend on field order. If someone reorders fields or inserts a new one, your values bind to the wrong fields (or fail to compile). Prefer keyed literals: Config{Host: "localhost", Port: 8080, TLS: true}.

checkpoints.prompt: Embed User into Admin so that an Admin gets the User's fields.
checkpoints.explanation: Writing just the type name `User` (no field name) embeds it. The User's fields and methods are then promoted, so admin.Name works directly. The other forms create named fields, which are not embedding.

codeLab.title: Mutate a struct through a pointer
codeLab.instructions: Given the `Account` type, implement `Deposit(a *Account, amount int)` that adds amount to a.Balance (ignoring negative amounts). Because you take a pointer, the caller's account is updated.
hints: Take *Account so changes reach the caller's struct.
Go auto-dereferences pointers, so a.Balance works without writing (*a).Balance.

debuggingLab.title: A method that won't change the struct
debuggingLab.symptom: After calling SetName, the counter's name is still empty.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A value receiver (c Counter) operates on a COPY of the struct. Assigning c.Name = n changes only that copy, which is discarded when the method returns, so the caller's Counter is untouched.
commonMistakes: Using a value receiver for a method that needs to mutate the struct.
Assuming methods always modify the underlying value.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Change SetName to a pointer receiver so it mutates the original.

theory.question: What are value semantics, and how do they apply to structs in Go?
theory.directAnswer: Value semantics mean that assigning a struct, passing it to a function, or returning it copies all of its fields. The copy is independent of the original, so mutating it does not affect the source. To let a function modify the caller's struct, pass a pointer (*T).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A rule that struct values are copied, not shared, on assignment and function calls.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It makes data flow explicit and prevents accidental shared-state mutation, which is a common bug source in reference-semantic languages.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler copies the contiguous bytes of the struct; passing &s instead shares the address so the callee can edit the original.

theory.whyImportant: It drives the value-vs-pointer-receiver decision and explains a whole class of 'my change didn't stick' bugs.
theory.realWorldExample: A function that updates a User's balance must take *User; taking User would update a discarded copy.

followUps.question: When should a method use a pointer receiver?
followUps.answer: When it must mutate the struct, or when the struct is large enough that copying it is wasteful. Be consistent across a type's method set.

followUps.question: Are small structs ever better passed by value?
followUps.answer: Yes — tiny, immutable-by-design structs are cheap to copy and can stay on the stack, avoiding heap allocation.

theory.question: What is struct embedding and how does it differ from inheritance?
theory.directAnswer: Embedding places one type inside another without a field name, promoting the embedded type's fields and methods so they are accessible directly on the outer type. It is composition, not inheritance: the outer type is not a subtype, there is no method overriding via dynamic dispatch on the embedded type, and you can still access the embedded value explicitly.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A composition mechanism that promotes an embedded type's members to the outer struct.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go favors composition over inheritance; embedding gives reuse without a class hierarchy.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler forwards field/method access to the embedded value; conflicts are resolved by the outer type's own members taking precedence.

theory.whyImportant: It is the idiomatic way to reuse behavior in Go and a frequent point of confusion for people from OO backgrounds.
theory.realWorldExample: Embedding sync.Mutex into a struct lets you call s.Lock() directly while keeping the struct's own fields.

followUps.question: What happens if the outer and embedded types both have a field named X?
followUps.answer: The outer type's X shadows the embedded one; you reach the embedded field explicitly via s.Embedded.X.

followUps.question: Does embedding satisfy interfaces?
followUps.answer: Yes — if an embedded type's promoted methods satisfy an interface, the outer type satisfies it too.

scenario.question: Your service mutates items in a slice of structs inside a range loop, but the changes never appear. What's the cause and the fix?
scenario.directAnswer: The range loop variable is a COPY of each struct element, so writing to it modifies the copy, not the slice element. Fix it by indexing the slice directly (s[i].Field = ...) or ranging to get the index and using it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A value-semantics trap: range over []T yields copies of structs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Structs are value types, so range copies each element into the loop variable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Mutating the loop variable updates the copy; indexing the slice updates the stored element in place.

scenario.whyImportant: It is a classic, easy-to-miss bug whenever you store structs (not pointers) in a slice.
scenario.realWorldExample: Looping `for _, item := range orders { item.Total = ... }` silently drops every update; `for i := range orders { orders[i].Total = ... }` fixes it.

followUps.question: Would a slice of pointers ([]*T) avoid this?
followUps.answer: Yes — ranging yields a copy of the pointer, but it still points at the same struct, so mutations through it are visible.

coding.question: Define a `Rectangle` struct and implement `func (r Rectangle) Area() int` and `func (r *Rectangle) Scale(factor int)`. Explain the receiver choice.
coding.thoughtProcess: Area only reads fields, so a value receiver is fine and conventional. Scale mutates the rectangle, so it needs a pointer receiver to change the caller's struct rather than a copy.
coding.lineByLine: Area reads Width and Height and returns their product; it doesn't mutate, so a value receiver is idiomatic. Scale multiplies both fields by factor; because it must change the original, it takes a pointer receiver so the caller's Rectangle is updated.

followUps.question: Can you call Scale on a non-addressable value?
followUps.answer: No — a pointer-receiver method needs an addressable value; Rectangle{2,3}.Scale(2) won't compile, but a variable r.Scale(2) will.

followUps.question: Should Area and Scale share the same receiver kind?
followUps.answer: It is good style to keep a type's method set consistent (all pointer or all value) when feasible, especially once any method needs a pointer.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Model domain entities as structs with clear, exported fields and use embedding for cross-cutting concerns (e.g., embedding a base Metadata struct). Keep API DTOs separate from internal models.
productionDeepDive.performance: Order fields to minimize alignment padding for large, numerous structs; pass big structs by pointer in hot paths to avoid copy costs while watching for unwanted heap escapes.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: A struct shared across goroutines needs synchronization for its mutable fields; embedding sync.Mutex (and guarding access) is a common pattern, but copying a struct that contains a Mutex is a bug.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Lean on the zero value: design structs so their zero value is a valid, usable state (e.g., bytes.Buffer), reducing initialization bugs.
productionDeepDive.observability: Use struct tags to drive JSON/log encoding consistently, and implement String() (Stringer) on key types for readable logs.
productionDeepDive.security: Be careful exporting fields that should be internal; use tags like json:"-" to keep secrets out of serialized output.

caseStudies.problem: Callers forgetting to initialize a buffer caused crashes in naive designs.
caseStudies.solution: Designed so the zero value is a ready-to-use empty buffer.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Requires careful field design but removes a whole class of init bugs.
caseStudies.lessons: A well-designed zero value makes structs safer and simpler to use.

keyTakeaways: A struct groups named fields into one value type; copying or passing it copies all fields.
Use keyed literals (T{Field: v}) and lean on the zero value, which sets every field to its own zero.
Use pointer receivers/parameters when a function or method must mutate the original struct.
Go has no inheritance — embed structs for composition, and use == comparability and field tags where appropriate.
